And Silicon Valley seems to be in the grip of a religious revival. When Pope Leo XIV issued an encyclical on A.I., he was alongside Christopher Olah, a co-founder of Anthropic. Garry Tan, the C.E.O. of the startup accelerator Y Combinator, hosted an event on how to integrate technology and Christianity. Anthropic recently convened a group of religious scholars to help determine whether Claude, its A.I. system, has a soul. Peter Thiel has spent the past year giving a series of secret lectures, from San Francisco to Rome, on Biblical prophecy. His theory is that anyone who wants to halt the development of A.I. is in league with the Antichrist. For A.I. optimists, we’re on the cusp of an earthly paradise—just build a big enough computer, and the Messianic age will arrive. No more death, no more suffering, privately owned galaxies for all. If you look at total cumulative emissions today, non-Al digital infrastructure-video streaming, enterprise cloud storage, social media, and traditional web hosting-still accounts for roughly three-quarters of all data center electricity and emissions. Attributing the entire 25.7 million tons in the Harvard study solely to Al

is factually inaccurate.

However, if you look at marginal emissions-

new power plants built because of load growth, Al is the primary driver. Traditional data center energy use stayed nearly flat between 2014 and 2017 because efficiency improvements matched demand growth. The sharp upward inflection since 2018-and the wave of behind-the-meter natural gas turbines and delayed coal retirements in states like Virginia, Louisiana, Ohio, and Texas-is overwhelmingly driven by high-density GPU campuses.

I've had early access to GPT 6.2 Astra for a few weeks and it is a weird but highly capable model. It's certainly the smartest model I've worked with in terms of raw intelligence but like a lot of very smart humans, it has a hard time communicating effectively. Most notably, I made some new and exciting historical discoveries with it (a first for me with an LLM...more soon) but here are some broad first impressions.
6.2 Astra excels at long running, largely autonomous knowledge-work tasks like indexing thousands of pages of documents, looking for sources in obscure places, or managing other agents to do actual research. Fable and Opus both do well at this too; but I've found that 6.2 Astra can figure out the full scope of the task I need it to accomplish, work laterally, and do the job in a way that, in my field, emulates the best human research work. I encountered no notable issues with accuracy or laziness in the work itself which is a first.

At the same time, 6.2 Astra also has a strange tendency to second guess its own conclusions and to summarize its actions in a misleading, backwards speak shorthand which often left me
*thinking* there were issues when it wasn't the case. That has been hard to get used to.
As I think @mattshumer_ and @emollick have both suggested, this is probably a post training issue as it's evident in the writing, not the actually research process. For example, 6.2
Astra will tell you it has completed a task and then proceed to breakdown that completeness into several layers of needless abstraction which gets overly confusing when the job is simply done, making it seem like parts remain to be done that were, in fact, completed quite well.
This seems to come from a lack of confidence in its own work which is completely unwarranted, in my experience. This also means that the model has a really weird tendency to avoid drawing firm conclusions on any of the non-deterministic tasks that I gave it involving qualitative evidence.

It's like if it can't quantify the answer numerically to produce a proof, it hedges. That is probably beneficial in frontier math, but in most knowledge work, the evidence is almost always going to be incomplete in some way and you have to eventually draw conclusions. As it said to me, it has a tendency to needlessly generalize from uncertainty about irrelevant details to larger conclusions that should be self-evident. More on that soon.
I didn't try it much with coding tasks so won't comment there.
All in all, 6.2 Astra is an extremely capable model, probably the most intelligent one I've used. But with this intelligence comes an annoying insecurity about its own abilities and judgement. I get the sense that it just needs to be a bit more confident and straight forward.
But if you can get past the weirdness, it's extremely useful, at least that's my experience.
